concepts.meaning: Fashion associated with the 1970s, marked by wide lapels, flares, and earth tones.
Fashion associated with the 1980s, marked by power shoulders and acid wash denim.
Fashion associated with the 1990s, marked by minimalism, grunge, and slip dresses.
Fashion associated with the 2000s, marked by low-rise jeans and logo-heavy branding.
A silhouette narrow at the shoulders that flares gradually outward toward the hem.
A series of narrow, uniform pleats that fold like the bellows of an accordion.
Denim treated with chlorine-soaked pumice for a high-contrast, marbled bleach effect.
Synthetic wool substitute used in knitwear.
A cuff or waist tab with multiple button positions that lets the wearer adjust the fit.
Wearable in any season.
A shoe toe rounded to a soft point, resembling an almond shape.
A soft, warm fiber shorn from alpacas, lighter and often silkier than sheep's wool.
A garment length ending at the ankle.
A shoe toe with a separate panel stitched across the top, resembling an apron.
An Irish cable-knit style named for the Aran Islands, combining braided and honeycomb patterns.
A garment sourced from a brand's or collector's historical holdings rather than current stock.
A pocket positioned on the sleeve of a jacket, common on military and utility outerwear.
A pre-curved knee panel with extra seaming that allows the leg to bend without pulling.
A sleeve pre-curved and paneled at the elbow to move naturally with a bent arm.
A hemline or garment edge deliberately uneven rather than level all the way around.
A front zipper placed off-center rather than running down the garment's midline.
Made for or styled after sport.
A carried container; handbags, totes, hobos, crossbodies.
A very loose, oversized trouser fit through both the seat and legs.
A thick, tightly woven nylon fabric originally developed for military flak vests, prized for abrasion resistance.
A silhouette that billows out full through the body and gathers in tightly at the hem.
An exaggeratedly rounded, voluminous sleeve gathered tightly at the wrist or above the elbow.
A short standing collar with no fold-over point, buttoned at the front.
A short, dense zigzag of stitches used to reinforce a stress point such as a pocket corner.
A single-layer shirt cuff that closes with one or more buttons, the standard everyday cuff.
A dyed fabric pattern made using a wax-resist technique originating in Indonesia.
A brimless knitted cap.
An extreme flare that widens sharply below the knee into a bell shape at the hem.
A sleeve fitted through the upper arm that flares gently outward from the elbow down.
A patch pocket with pleated side panels that expand outward to hold bulky items.
A strap worn around the waist.
A garment cinched at the waist with a fabric belt threaded through loops or a self-tie.
A garment cut diagonally across the fabric grain so it drapes and clings with natural stretch.
An asymmetric-zip leather jacket with lapels, from motorcycle wear.
A woven pattern of small diamond shapes with a center dot, resembling a bird's eye.
A long sleeve that is fuller at the bottom than the top and gathered into a cuff.
A shoe construction adding a protective midsole layer to a Blake stitch for extra durability.
A shoe construction stitching the upper directly to the sole through a single seam, giving a sleeker profile.
A tailored jacket worn without matching trousers.
A hem stitched so the thread is hidden inside the fold and barely visible from the outside.
Leather with an exaggerated, raised pebbled grain that looks like blisters across the surface.
A thick, sturdy heel of uniform width from top to bottom.
A loose woven top, usually women's.
A wide, shallow neckline that runs almost straight across the front from shoulder to shoulder.
Knitted wool felted through heat and agitation into a dense, springy fabric.
A waist-length jacket with ribbed hem and cuffs, from military flight jackets.
A trouser leg that stays slim through the knee and flares slightly at the hem to clear a boot.
Footwear covering the foot and ankle or more.
A fabric woven or knitted from looped, curled yarn, giving a nubby textured surface.
A seam whose raw edges are enclosed in a folded strip of binding fabric or tape.
A pleat formed by two folds turned away from each other, creating a flat panel between them.
A fit that is squared off and roomy through the body, with little shaping at the waist.
A closure where a frame and prong hold a strap in place, as on belts and boots.
An exaggerated spread collar with very wide, long points that fan out like wings.
A trouser fly that closes with a row of buttons instead of a zipper.
A front opening closed by buttons.
A collar with buttonholes on the points that fasten the collar down to the shirt body.
A knit with raised, twisted rope-like columns formed by crossing stitches over each other.
A fine-grained leather from young cattle, softer and smoother than adult cowhide.
An open, unstructured collar that lies flat against the shirt with no button at the throat.
A heavy, tightly woven plain-weave cotton or linen cloth prized for durability.
A soft, brimmed or peaked hat.
A very short sleeve that covers only the top of the shoulder without extending past the armpit.
A shoe with a separate leather panel stitched across the toe box.
A knitted top that opens down the front.
Trousers with large bellows pockets on the legs.
Sturdy workwear trousers with a hammer loop and a wide tool pocket on one thigh.
A trouser leg cut full at the hip and thigh that tapers sharply to a narrow ankle.
A fine, soft fiber combed from the undercoat of cashmere goats.
Informal, everyday dressing.
A shoe construction bonding the upper to the sole with adhesive rather than stitching.
A looped stitch formed by one thread that produces a decorative, slightly stretchy seam.
A hem sewn on a chain-stitch machine that produces a rope-like puckered edge as it ages.
A pattern of soft, slightly blurred vertical stripes resembling chalk lines on a suiting cloth.
A lightweight plain-weave fabric with a colored warp and white weft, resembling light denim.
Patterned with crossing lines.
An ankle boot with elastic side gussets and no laces, easy to slip on.
A fabric woven with a fuzzy, caterpillar-like pile yarn, soft and dimensional to the touch.
A small pocket positioned on the upper chest of a jacket or shirt.
A lightweight, sheer, plain-weave fabric with a slightly rough, matte feel.
Cotton twill trousers, flat or pleated.
A shoe toe squared off with flat, angled sides, resembling a chisel tip.
Leather tanned with chromium salts, faster to produce and softer than vegetable tanning.
An ankle-high leather or suede boot with open lacing, typically two or three eyelets.
An adjustable strap or elastic panel at the center back waist that draws the garment in.
A peak lapel with the point rounded off into a soft clover-like curve.
A shirt collar with rounded, curved points instead of sharp corners.
A knee-length or longer outer layer.
A rounded silhouette full through the middle and tapered at both the shoulders and hem.
A small compartment set inside a larger pocket, originally sized for a pocket watch or coins.
Has a collar.
Has no collar.
Solid blocks of contrasting colour.
A slim, straight silhouette running the same width from shoulder to hem.
Topstitching sewn in a thread color that deliberately contrasts with the base fabric.
A dense, non-porous leather from the fibrous shell layer of a horse's hindquarters.
A ribbed pile fabric with raised parallel cords called wales running its length.
A footbed layer of compressed cork that molds slightly to the foot over time.
A button carved from the corozo palm nut, prized for its natural grain and sheen.

A pull-on boot with a pointed toe and underslung heel, originally designed for riding.
The most common leather, from adult cattle, valued for its durability and abundance.
A loosely draped, soft fold of fabric at the neckline that hangs in folds rather than standing.
A soft, textured natural rubber sole with a light, springy feel.
A round, close-fitting neckline that sits at the base of the neck without a collar.
Leather finished or treated so the surface wrinkles into a fine crinkled texture.
A garment cut shorter than standard, ending above the natural hip or waist.
A medium-height heel with straight sides that does not curve inward like a stiletto.
A belt or strap closure using two D-shaped metal rings that the strap threads through and back.

A stitched, wedge-shaped fold that removes fabric fullness to shape a garment to the body.
Unsold, unused merchandise that has sat in inventory since its original release.
A garment left with exposed seams, raw edges, or unfinished elements as a design choice.
A soft, supple leather from deer, traditionally used in gloves and moccasins.
Sturdy warp-faced cotton twill, usually indigo; the cloth of jeans and truckers.
A shoe with open lacing, where the eyelet tabs are sewn on top of the vamp.
A designer's secondary, more affordable collection sold under a related label name.
Leather deliberately treated to look aged, scuffed, or weathered before sale.
A sleeve with a very deep armhole cut in one with the bodice, tapering narrow at the wrist.
An Irish tweed with flecks of contrasting color, historically dyed with local plant dyes.
A workwear trouser construction with a second layer of fabric stitched over each knee for durability.

A jacket or coat front with two parallel columns of buttons and overlapping fronts.
Insulated with bird down.
A British four-color disruptive camouflage pattern using irregular blotches.

A cord run through a channel at a hem, hood, or waist that cinches the opening when pulled.
A one-piece garment covering the torso and hanging over the legs.
A construction where the shoulder seam sits below the natural shoulder line, giving a relaxed hang.
A silhouette with the waistline seam lowered to sit at or below the hip.
A mottled brown and green camouflage pattern originally issued to US paratroopers in WWII.
A very tightly woven, heavyweight plain-weave cotton fabric, sturdier than canvas.
A British term for denim bib overalls or, informally, for jeans generally.
Elastic fibre blended in for stretch.
Decorated with needlework.
A silhouette with a raised waistline sitting just below the bust, falling loosely to the hem.
A pull-on leather work boot with a strap and buckle at the ankle and calf instead of laces.

A zipper sewn so its teeth and tape show on the garment's face rather than being concealed.

Pile fabric imitating fur.
Plastic-coated fabric imitating leather.
A dense, textured wool knit traditionally worn by fishermen, often combining cables and seed stitch.
A notch lapel variant with an exaggeratedly wide, rounded notch resembling an open fish mouth.

A jetted or welt pocket finished with a rectangular flap of fabric covering the opening.
A trouser leg that widens gradually from the knee to a wide hem.

A platform sole of even thickness from heel to toe, with no heel elevation.
A seam stitched so the two fabric edges lie flat side by side rather than overlapping.

A hem falling all the way to the floor.

For formal occasions.

A garment lined completely on the inside, concealing all interior seams.

A waterproof, breathable membrane laminated into outerwear fabric.
A pictorial or text design on the piece.
A natural, honey-colored rubber sole common on desert boots and casual shoes.

A garment length ending at or just below the hip bone.

A short, slender heel of about one to two inches with a slight curve.
A garment length ending at the knee.

Fabric made by interlooping yarn.
Closed by laces threaded through eyelets.

A jacket cut in leather.

Sleeves reaching the wrist.
